source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 60: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer: Assumptions: the GPU model, framework/runtime version, precision, allocator, tensor/pipeline parallel layout, maximum sequence length, batch policy, cache policy, and request mix are not specified; record them before drawing conclusions. Treat an OOM as a measured event, not proof of a single cause. Prioritize a synchronized per-request timeline: capture prompt and generated-token lengths, active sequences, batch membership, KV-cache bytes/pages and growth rate, reserved versus allocated GPU memory, largest free block/fragmentation, weights, activations, workspace, CUDA/NCCL allocations, and host-side limits. First check whether one request exceeds its context/max-position limit, whether concurrency or continuous batching admits too many long sequences, and whether KV growth matches the expected bytes-per-token; then isolate allocator fragmentation, leaked/stale cache pages, temporary workspaces, and topology/replication effects. Preserve a minimal crash-free baseline and a deterministic replay of the failing seed and arrival schedule. Falsifiable hypothesis: the intermittent OOM is caused primarily by concurrent KV growth beyond the usable per-device budget (possibly amplified by fragmentation); under the same request/token trace, a measured admission limit or paged KV allocation with reserved headroom prevents OOM without unacceptable correctness or SLO regression. Falsify it if OOM persists with bounded KV occupancy and defragmented allocations, or if telemetry attributes the peak to another component. Compare baseline with one change at a time across warmup and repeated randomized trials, recording OOM/error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, TTFT/TPOT, utilization, memory high-water marks, fragmentation, and output correctness. Mitigations should be staged conservatively: cap concurrent tokens/sequences and maximum context, reject or queue requests before allocation, reserve safety headroom, use paged KV/prefix reuse only after validating isolation and eviction behavior, and consider precision reduction or quantization only with quality and kernel compatibility tests. Roll back on any correctness change, OOM, error/timeout increase, memory headroom breach, or agreed SLO violation; do not claim a fix without raw synchronized traces, repeated reproduction results, allocator/cache telemetry, and canary/rollback records.
